title: Validation of a Hybrid Physics-Informed Machine Learning Model for Mobile Radiation Detection Using Monte Carlo N-Particle Simulations
abstract: Accurate estimation of the Maximum Detectable Distance (MDD) is essential for reliable mobile gamma spectrometry in environmental radiation monitoring and post-remediation surveying. Conventional analytical and data-driven approaches may have limited predictive accuracy under dynamic conditions involving detector motion, photon attenuation, and varying background radiation. A physics-informed neural network (PINN) was developed to estimate MDD by integrating radiation transport relationships with simulation and field data. The model incorporates inverse-square geometric spreading and exponential photon attenuation through physics-based constraints in the training objective, while MCNP 5 -derived photon transport data inform attenuation behavior. Detector velocity, source-to-detector distance, and background count rate serve as primary inputs. The framework also incorporates velocity-dependent dwell-time effects and Monte Carlo-based uncertainty analysis. The approach was evaluated using field-acquired mobile gamma spectrometry measurements and site-specific MCNP 5 simulations representing 662 keV photon transport through silicate-rich soil. Results demonstrate that physics-based constraints and MCNP-informed attenuation behavior improve MDD prediction performance and generalization across varying survey conditions. Relative to conventional approaches, the hybrid model reduced MDD prediction errors by approximately 10-30%, with the greatest improvements observed at higher detector velocities. The proposed framework provides a physics-guided approach for MDD estimation to support mobile radiation detection, survey planning, and environmental radiological assessment.

title: The evolution of computer codes for the analysis of severe accidents in light water reactors, WASH-1400 to present
abstract: This paper describes the evolution of our understanding of the potential consequences of severe accidents in light water based on research and model development undertaken by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission through its contractors and by the U.S. nuclear industry. Major milestones were activities undertaken by Brookhaven National Laboratory in support of the WASH-740 study, based on a very limited experimental database, by AEC contractors in support of the Reactor Safety Study (WASH-1400), which was the first major attempt to quantify the risk to the public from severe accidents, to the follow-on NUREG-1150 risk study and most recently to the insights provided by the NRC's SOARCA program. The Three Mile Island Unit-2 accident, which shortly followed after the release of WASH-1400, provided impetus to the regulatory authority and the regulated industry to perform research to better understand the potential frequency and consequences of severe accidents. This paper describes the development of the tools used to predict accident consequences based on research performed by the NRC (and its contractors) and by the nuclear industry (including the Electric Power Research Institute). Over time, these tools have matured, have been validated against research results, and have gained a level of configuration management enabling them to be used in demonstrating safety adequacy for the licensing and regulatory oversight of these reactors. This paper has been limited in its scope to severe accident analysis development activities in the U.S.

title: Direct numerical simulation of turbulent natural convection in a heat generating fluid within a shallow horizontal enclosure
abstract: Core catchers are a significant safety feature of Generation-IV nuclear reactors for the safe dissipation of decay heat and maintaining the integrity of the reactor containment in the event of a severe accident. Direct numerical simulation is used to simulate turbulent natural convection in a shallow layer of dense oxidic corium, with significant internal heat generation ( R a i = 4.5 × 1 0 8 ), at the base of a core catcher. The simulation revealed a large persistent convection cell adjacent to the pitched lateral boundary, smaller eddies comparable in dimension to the fluid depth closer to the centre of the core catcher and enhanced dissipation of turbulent kinetic energy in the upper half of the fluid. Around 73 % of the heat generated within the fluid is dissipated from the upper boundary. The surface and time-averaged heat flux at the upper and lower boundaries are in good agreement with Emara and Kulacki predictions in the shallow limit. Significant spatiotemporal fluctuations in local Nusselt number are observed, with local flares in heat flux manifesting in local Nusselt numbers of several times the surface average. These local flares are less frequent at the lower and lateral boundaries but greater in amplitude relative to the surface-averaged heat flux. Further research is required into the duration and frequency of these flares, given the potential of persistent local flares to induce crust remelting or localised thermal attack of the core catcher.

title: Burnup-dependent nuclear safeguards and security assessment of HALEU-Fueled sodium-cooled fast reactors
abstract: This study presents a burnup- and cooling-time-dependent assessment of safeguards- and security-relevant characteristics of spent fuel from high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU)-fueled sodium-cooled fast reactors (SFRs). A physics-based framework is adopted to evaluate spent fuel in terms of three functions: material attractiveness, self-protection, and monitorability. Within this framework, decay heat, photon emission rate, spontaneous fission rate, and external dose rate are treated as key spent-fuel attributes that collectively determine safeguards and security functions. Burnup-dependent isotopic inventories were generated using the Serpent 2 Monte Carlo code and tracked through post-discharge decay. The resulting isotopic compositions were further used in photon and neutron transport calculations to quantify radiation signatures and dose rates over cooling times ranging from 1 day to 100 years. For reference and verification, analyses were also performed for a conventional low-enriched uranium pressurized water reactor (PWR) and a recycled-fuel SFR. Results show that material attractiveness, self-protection, and monitorability exhibit strong dependence on both discharge burnup and cooling time. The fast neutron spectrum of the HALEU-fueled SFR limits the buildup of higher-mass transuranic isotopes such as 244 Cm, resulting in comparatively weak spontaneous-fission neutron signatures and negligible neutron dose contributions. Consequently, radiological self-protection is dominated by photon-emitting isotopes, and passive neutron monitoring may be less effective than photon-based approaches. Higher-burnup fuel maintains greater decay heat, photon emission rates, and dose rates at long cooling times, resulting in stronger intrinsic barriers and enhanced monitorability. These results demonstrate the importance of accounting for the combined effects of discharge burnup and post-discharge cooling time on spent-fuel characteristics when developing safeguards and physical protection strategies for advanced reactor systems.

title: Research on control rod cusping effect correction methods in the 2D/1D transport calculations
abstract: The cusping effect is one of the critical challenges that must be addressed in the reactor core physics simulations involving control rod movement. This study proposes two improved methods for correcting the control rod cusping effect in the 2D/1D transport calculations. First, the conventional Both Axial and Radial Homogenization (BARH) method in NECP-X is enhanced by subdividing partially rodded axial planes into sub-planes, each undergoing independent radial homogenization. The radial leakage term of each sub-plane was then approximated using the leakage terms of its adjacent layers. Second, an Axial-Only Homogenization (AOH) method was developed, building on the material-region-based 2D/1D transport method. This method leverages high-precision axial fine-mesh fluxes from material regions to perform flux-volume-weighted axial homogenization. It initially approximates the radial leakage terms of sub-planes using those of adjacent layers, and further refines these terms via pre-calculated radial leakage correction factors. Validation of the proposed methods was performed on the VERA #4 and VERA #5 benchmarks, and on the SPERT 3 × 3 assembly and full-core problems. Results show that, compared with the conventional BARH method, the improved BARH method significantly improves the correction accuracy of the cusping effect and demonstrates strong potential for application to typical commercial PWR control rod clusters. For problems involving large, strong-absorber control rods in the research reactors, the AOH method combined with radial leakage correction achieves the highest accuracy, meeting the precision requirements for correcting the cusping effect in research reactors.

title: Numerical study on capacitive metal rod position detector in double-layer medium
abstract: Position signals of control rods are important parameters that should be measured during the operation of nuclear reactors. The performance of capacitive detectors for measuring control rod positions in a double-layer medium is numerically studied in this paper. According to the experimental results of concave electrodes capacitive detectors, the numerical model is verified. The mathematical expression of the detector signal is derived as a function of rod position and liquid level. The error characteristics of the capacitive detectors for measuring the eccentric metal rod are revealed. The method for evaluating measuring errors of capacitive detectors in double-layer medium is constructed. The relation between flare angles of electrodes and measuring errors is studied, and the optimization method of the flare angles is discussed. The design of the integrated capacitive metal rod position detector (CMRPD) is proposed. Measuring errors and performance of the detector are evaluated.

title: Experimental investigation of corium top-flooding with sustained induction heating and MCCI
abstract: Top-flooding of molten prototypic corium is investigated experimentally, in the presence of sustained induction heating of the melt. The melt lays on the top of a concrete layer, and consecutively to the sustained heating, molten-core concrete interaction (MCCI) occurs. The experiment is conducted in the MERELAVA facility, which enables to melt and study oxidic and steel corium (using thermite reaction or thermite plus induction heating, with a maximum capacity of 80 kg of corium). The steam flowrate generated after corium flooding is quantified through a vapor line made of a condenser and condensate tank. In the present test, the initial corium mixture is composed of 54%UO 2 /23%ZrO 2 /8%Concrete/15%Steel (weight percentage). The water is injected in several batches. After an initial phase of dry ablation of the siliceous concrete, several water injections on the top of the melt have been realized with a total volume of 74 liters. We present an overview of the experimental setup and a summary of test conditions carried out in the facility. Steam flowrate is measured by condensing the steam and measuring the condensate mass flowrate. Heat flux estimates are provided, based on the mass flowrate analysis and heat exchanger data. Dismantling observations of the solidified ingot are also given.

title: CFD investigation of gas-core instability in axial swirl separators using a coupled VOF-two-fluid model
abstract: Unstable flow in gas–liquid separators significantly degrades separation efficiency and system reliability. While previous work has documented unstable flow phenomena, the statistical regularities of transient interfacial oscillations and their quantitative coupling with local flow parameters (swirl intensity, pressure gradient, and velocity slip) have not been fully quantified. To address these gaps, the present study develops and validates a coupled VOF-two-fluid model for axial swirl separators, incorporating the Reynolds Stress Model (RSM) to investigate the dynamic characteristics of transient gas-core behavior. The results show that under unstable conditions, the gas core exhibits quasi-periodic “necking-expansion” oscillations with bimodal probability distributions (peaks at 29.56 mm and 36.49 mm), contrasting sharply with the unimodal distribution observed under stable flow. The standard deviation of core diameter increases by 116% (from 1.8 mm to 3.9 mm), quantitatively confirming fluctuation amplification. Strong negative correlations are observed between core diameter and swirl intensity, with swirl intensity decaying by approximately 4% during an expansion event at Z/D = 8. Transient pressure-drop peaks reach 4.62 times the temporal mean and are synchronized with core oscillations, indicating strong pressure-interface coupling. Swirl intensity decays monotonically along the axis, by 47% from its maximum after an axial length of 10D, while velocity slip remains elevated in the region of Z/D = 3–13. This competition between weakening centrifugal constraints and sustained shear effects drives instability onset in the middle-to-downstream region, which is characterized by the proposed dimensionless stability indicator (We/Nc). These findings provide additional insight into gas-core instability behavior.

title: Investigation of Performance of a Large-Scale Water-Based RCCS Under Varying Decay Heat Loads
abstract: The objective of the present study is to investigate the effects of varying decay heat loads and tank inlet elevations on the performance of a large-scale water-based reactor cavity cooling system (RCCS) utilizing the water-based Natural convection Shutdown heat removal Test Facility (NSTF) at Argonne National Laboratory. A power parametric series with prototypic decay heat loads of 1.4 MWt, 1.75 MWt, 2.1 MWt, and 2.4 MWt) (34.4 kWt, 43.0 kWt, 51.6 kWt, and 58.5 kWt scaled) with a low tank inlet configuration was tested.The system performance metrics at the two-phase quasi-steady state were compared, mainly the system flow, steam generation rate, system pressure, and liquid and structure temperatures. The effect of the decay heat power level on the boiling front progression was also investigated.It was found that lower decay heat loads caused delayed boiling front progression. The results were then compared to previous data sets collected at identical testing conditions but with chimney piping configured at the mid tank elevation configuration. Overall, the tank inlet elevation did not significantly influence the system two-phase quasi-steady-state performance at the studied decay heat levels. However, the tank inlet elevation had a significant impact on the two-phase flow instability characteristics and the boiling front propagation.A static flashing model identified from the literature predicted the flow oscillation period well but would result in high flashing superheating. Additional analysis also identified the presence of Type-I density wave oscillations (DWOs) in the present study. By plotting all the test results on the subcooling and Zuber plane, a chimney exit quality of ~0.3% was identified as a trigger for the onset of flow oscillations.

title: Structural integrity assessment and manufacturability-oriented design improvement of the HCCP TBM shield
abstract: The Helium Cooled Ceramic Pebble (HCCP) TBM shield is a safety-important component (SIC-1) serving as a vacuum boundary and the first confinement barrier, and a design with a simplified internal structure has been proposed to improve its manufacturability. In this study, a structural integrity assessment of the simplified HCCP TBM shield was performed in accordance with RCC-MRx 2018, considering 15 single loads and 17 load combinations. The assessment covers all operating states, namely the normal operation state (NOS), the baking state, and the tritium outgassing state (TOS), as well as the electromagnetic and seismic loads. While sufficient margins were confirmed for the accidental loads, negative margins were found in the load combinations governed by the pressure in the baking state, identifying the baking state as the design driver of the TBM shield. The cause was analyzed to be the combination of the reduction in the allowable stress intensity at the elevated temperature of 240 °C and the increased bending stresses of the walls caused by the enlarged spacing between the internal plates. In the design improvement for the margin recovery, manufacturability was consistently applied as a decision criterion. Parameter studies on the side wall thickness, the front plate thickness, and the pipe casing layout were performed for an improved geometry in which the width of the shield block containing the pipe casing bends was increased, and it was confirmed that the combination of a 40 mm side wall and a front plate of 60 mm or thicker recovers the structural integrity in all shield blocks. In addition, it was quantitatively shown that the pipe casings act as structural stiffeners and that their reinforcing effect increases with the symmetry of the casing layout. These results provide a design solution reconciling the structural integrity with the manufacturability without reintroducing the internal plates, and a quantitative basis for the geometry optimization in the final design phase.

title: Robustness of moving-window Ib-value analysis for acoustic-emission-based fracture precursor detection under severe background noise
abstract: Background noise in operating nuclear power plants masks the acoustic emission (AE) signals of micro-cracks and hinders early fracture-precursor detection. A moving-window Ib-value methodology is proposed and validated by a proof-of-concept tensile test on a notched SM45C carbon steel specimen. For 651 crack signals screened by source location, the energy-based b-value (Aki's maximum likelihood method) and the Ib-value were evaluated, and detection-threshold elevation was emulated by removing up to 50% of the low-amplitude data. The cumulative approach diluted the precursor and never reached the alarm criterion of 1.0, whereas the 100-hit moving window immediately captured the shift of the crack mode from shear to tensile. Under increasing noise, low-amplitude micro-crack signals were selectively lost (survival 100% to 40%, against 100% for macro-cracks), biasing the b-value by up to −19.8%, while the Ib-value, which evaluates only the distribution's statistical center, stayed within ±4.9%. Across 0–40% hit loss it still crossed the criterion 7.4–11.8 s before rupture, at 98.4–99.3% of peak stress. The moving-window Ib-value is therefore markedly less sensitive than the b-value to the selective loss of low-amplitude AE events caused by threshold elevation. Generalization to full background-noise robustness, which also involves waveform superposition and parameter distortion, requires further validation.

title: Geant4-Based Differentiable Optimization for Energy-Response Flattening of a Multi-Detector Neutron Long Counter
abstract: To address the significant energy dependence of long neutron counter responses in wide-energy-range fluence measurements, this paper proposes a differentiable-optimization-based method for flattening the energy response of a multi-detector long neutron counter. A Geant4 model of the multi-detector long counter was developed, and the energy–position response matrix of this detector was constructed for the energy range of 1 eV to 20 MeV. The relative standard deviation (RSD) of the synthesized response was used as the flatness metric, and two optimization approaches—discrete combinatorial search and differentiable continuous optimization—were compared. The results show that multi-position response synthesis effectively improves the response flatness of the long counter across a broad energy range. For a detector array with K = 8, the sampled combinatorial-search benchmark identified a configuration with an RSD of 3.79%, whereas differentiable optimization yielded 2.98%, indicating a lower RSD under the present calculation settings. Additionally, embedding tungsten rods in the moderator of a long neutron counter was found to improve the overall flatness of its response. Independent verification simulations were performed by placing 6 Li micro-detectors at the eight optimized axial positions, yielding a verified RSD of 2.84%. This study demonstrates that the proposed method effectively enhances the wide-energy-range response consistency of the multi-detector long counter and provides a reproducible computational framework for position optimization in such detector systems.

title: Development and Verification of an Efficient 3-D Finite Element Analysis Model for Irradiation Deformation of the Fast Reactor Fuel Assembly
abstract: The existing performance analysis of the fast reactor fuel assembly faces the challenge of balancing high-fidelity and computational efficiency. This study develops a 3-D irradiation deformation analysis model based on ABAQUS to address this conflict. The model employs shell elements to simulate claddings and the hexagonal duct, beam elements for wrap wires, and simplifies complex mechanical interactions using Tie Constraint, Axial Connector element, and General Contact. User subroutines are implemented to incorporate material irradiation behaviors and the non-uniform operating conditions. A parametric automatic modeling method is also developed to construct simplified structures and mechanical interactions. The analysis model has been verified against out-of-pile compression test for a 127-pin fuel bundle and an irradiation deformation benchmark case for a 169-pin fuel assembly, with verification parameters such as gap variation and ovalization. Results demonstrate good agreement with errors within 20%. Furthermore, compared with the simplified model in BAMBOO, the present model demonstrates higher accuracy in the simulation of mechanical interactions and possesses the capability to capture cladding circumferential effects; compared with the full-scale detailed model, the present model achieves comparable results while improving solution speed by over 100-fold for a 7-pin fuel assembly. This model is reliable, efficient and easily extensible for irradiation deformation analysis and design optimization of fast reactor fuel assemblies.

title: Comparing advanced model and human observers for CT detectability index under varied tube currents and contrasts
abstract: Objective This study aims to compare the detectability index (d′) between the human observer (HO) and advanced model observer (AMO) using the Non-Prewhitening Observer (NPW) and Non-Prewhitening Observer with Eye Filter (NPWE) for various tube currents and low-contrast objects. Methods Image data were obtained using the ACR 464 phantom at three different tube current levels (i.e., 80 mA, 140 mA, and 200 mA). The task object had contrast levels ranging from 3 HU to 15 HU, with a diameter of 3 mm. The task objects used a Gaussian profile model. The d′ values were measured using the AMO with NPW and NPWE models, while HO values were computed using the 2-AFC method. Each configuration consisted of 100 signal-present and 100 signal-absent images. Results The results demonstrated that the d′ values obtained from AMO displayed a trend similar to those derived from HO. Increases in the tube current and contrast resulted in higher d′ values across all observers. Correlation analysis revealed that NPW and NPWE showed a strong relationship with HO ( r = 0.979; p < 0.001) and ( r = 0.976; p < 0.001), respectively. Conclusion This study confirms that the AMO can effectively replicate object detection with accuracy comparable to that of HO. This behaviour was consistently observed across variations in tube current and low-contrast objects.

title: Assessment of occupational radiation exposure from gamma-emitting rad ionuclides in the bio-shield of Kori Unit 1 during decommissioning
abstract: The external dose to the workers of bio-shield of the Kori Unit 1 was evaluated by using the VISIPLAN 4.0 code to secure the radiation safety of its decommissioning work. In particular, radionuclide-specific activity concentration data, derived from prior MCNP simulations, were used to model three-dimensional radiation work scenarios. Each scenario was simulated with shielding and sampling configurations to calculate the external dose rates. Worker operation times were estimated based on the ICRP-recommendation and Nuclear Safety Act of annual average dose limit of 20 mSv. Variations in worker role, position, and task duration resulted in substantial disparities in individual cumulative doses. The maximum dose rate in scenario 1 under the 8-year cooling condition was 2.3 × 10 −1 mSv/h at 3 m height, decreasing to 9.3 × 10 −2 mSv/h under the 15-year condition (∼60 % reduction). A 20 mm lead shield reduced the dose rate by ∼86 %. The total dose rate in scenario 2 under the 8 year cooling condition was 1.33 × 10 1 mSv of workers 1 and 2, ∼22 times that of Worker 3. The minimum required shielding thickness was estimated at 14.8 mm. The allowable number of complete sampling operations was 32 and 80 for the 8 and 15 year cooling conditions, respectively.

title: Reinforcement learning for BWR fuel management
abstract: Boiling water reactor (BWR) core design is a highly constrained optimization problem that directly affects fuel costs in operating reactors. The problem consists of both fuel bundle design and core loading pattern design, each of which presents significant computational and combinatorial challenges. Historically, stochastic optimization methods such as genetic algorithms and simulated annealing have been the most widely used approaches for automated bundle and core design. More recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising class of algorithms capable of solving complex design problems while exploiting underlying physics-based patterns. This work presents a reinforcement learning framework for both fuel bundle and loading pattern optimization and demonstrates a sequential approach to BWR core design. First, the performance of the loading pattern optimizer is evaluated independently by reproducing a historic fuel cycle from an operating reactor using industry-designed assemblies. The optimizer consistently meets all cycle constraints and statistically outperforms the reference loading pattern, as demonstrated by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The full sequential optimization framework is then applied to design new fuel bundles and corresponding loading patterns for the same cycle. These results demonstrate that reinforcement learning can effectively address the sequential bundle and core design problem and highlight its potential to reduce design time and fuel costs in BWR core optimization.
title_ko: BWR 연료 관리를 위한 보강 학습

title: Development of new lead-free borate glasses: Experimental evaluation for the impact of BaO on radiation shielding properties of glasses
abstract: This study investigated advanced glass compositions for gamma-ray shielding consisting of (78-x) B 2 O 3 -8MgO-13ZnO-1Eu 2 O 3 -xBaO, x = 23, 26, 29, and 32 mol%. Attenuation coefficients were calculated experimentally and simulated. The results between the two methods are fairly similar, with a ± 5 % experimental–measured data difference. The addition of BaO improves the shielding performance of the prepared BMZE glass. The progression of the BaO concentration from 23 to 32 mol% within the prepared BMZE glasses causes an improvement in their LACs from 0.299 to 0.319 cm −1 at 661.7 keV and shows a consistent improvement over the examined gamma-ray energy range of 59.5–1332 keV. It is shown that the BMZE1–BMZE4 glass samples exhibited superior protection performance to RS 323 G19 lead-based shielding commercial glass, which contains 33 % lead oxide and 1.8 % cerium oxide, while BMZE4 exhibited superior protection performance to RS 360 lead-based shielding commercial glass, which contains 45 % lead oxide. Therefore, the prepared BMZE4 glass represents a lead-free shielding glass alternative for hospital nuclear medicine applications.

title: Numerical study of functionally graded material models for evaluation of thermomechanical loading on nuclear fuel particles
abstract: Functionally graded materials (FGMs) are well suited for analyzing the thermomechanical behavior of dispersed fuel particles under severe thermal and mechanical conditions, due to their capability to exhibit continuously varying properties in the radial direction. In this study, the primary focus is placed on the numerical analysis of an FGM hollow sphere subjected to thermal loading and internal pressure, as this configuration is more relevant to higher burnup conditions and the associated buildup of internal gas pressure. Within this framework, the radial distribution of material properties is assumed to be continuous, and the influence of the inhomogeneity parameter, β, on the temperature field, radial displacement, and radial and circumferential stresses is investigated. The results show that variations in β play a decisive role in the thermomechanical response of the hollow sphere and can alter both the magnitude and the radial location of stress concentration. Accordingly, an appropriate choice of β can be used to optimize the mechanical response of the fuel particle and reduce stress concentration in critical regions. The FGM solid-sphere formulation is included as a complementary theoretical formulation representing a physically relevant configuration for the early stage of irradiation; however, the parametric numerical results and quantitative discussion of the present study are restricted to the hollow-sphere configuration.

title: Effect of vertical heat exchange tube/tube-bundle condensation on aerosol diffusiophoretic deposition
abstract: During a severe accident, substantial amounts of radioactive aerosols are released into the containment. Upon activation of the Passive Containment Cooling System, these aerosols are driven by diffusiophoresis toward condensing heat exchange surfaces, thereby altering the distribution of radioactive inventory within the containment. This study experimentally investigates aerosol diffusiophoresis under single-tube and tube-bundle condensation conditions. A series of experiments on aerosol diffusiophoresis were conducted under systematically varied steam mole fractions, condensation rates, and system pressures, with real-time monitoring of the spatial aerosol concentration. The results indicate that particle size has a negligible effect on the diffusiophoresis velocity, an increased steam condensation rate enhances the deposition, while a reduction in steam mole fraction inhibits it. A higher steam density inhibits the diffusiophoresis velocity. Furthermore, the study investigates diffusiophoresis under both single-tube and tube-bundle condensation conditions. The effective deposition area coefficient (α), correlated with condensation rate and steam mole fraction, is proposed to modify the classical model, thereby improving its predictive accuracy. The study proposed the effective deposition area coefficient α, related to both the steam condensation rate and steam mole fraction, to modify the classical diffusiophoresis model. This correction effectively reduces the deviation between experimental data and model predictions, significantly improving the accuracy of diffusiophoresis decay constant forecasts under strong heat-sink tube-bundle condensation conditions. The findings provide essential experimental data and a refined model for assessing post-accident radioactivity distribution within the containment.
title_ko: 수직 열교환 튜브/튜브 번들 응축이 에어로졸 확산성 증착에 미치는 영향

title: An Integer Programming Method for Maintenance Schedule Optimization in Nuclear Power Plants
abstract: Maintenance scheduling in nuclear power plants (NPPs) is challenging because multicomponent systems exhibit strong interdependencies and must satisfy strict safety requirements. We present a two-tier framework that couples a mixed-integer programming (MIP) model with a probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) layer for at-power maintenance scheduling.The PRA module evaluates incumbent schedules, and through a solver callback, triggers additional constraints that exclude configurations violating PRA-derived risk thresholds, technical specification limits (e.g., limiting condition for operation windows), and physical work control rules, thereby guiding the MIP toward cost-optimal, safety-compliant solutions.We construct anonymized test sets by mapping real maintenance work packages onto a hypothetical high-pressure injection system comprised of three trains. The framework is validated on three weekly workloads (A-, B-, and C-train task sets), each examined under three backlog policies.With a 16-h wall-clock limit and interim checkpoints at 30 min, the framework proves optimality in three of nine scenarios and terminates within 10% of the best bound in all nine, with the backlog-enabled scenarios remaining the most numerically challenging (gaps of 3.32% to 9.10%), reflecting the added combinatorial difficulty of optional task selection.In a representative comparison against a schedule hand constructed by methods used in current practice, the optimized A-train plan satisfies all operational requirements at substantially lower labor cost ($28 920 versus $36 612) while respecting out-of-service limits and PRA guardrails.These results demonstrate that integrating MIP with configuration risk screening can reduce operating and maintenance costs without sacrificing safety margins, and represent a promising direction for further development toward routine, cost aware maintenance planning in NPPs.

title: On-line quantification of delayed neutron precursor drift reactivity in molten salt reactors: A shadow-precursor observer verified against closed-form benchmarks in Modelica/TRANSFORM
abstract: In molten salt reactors the delayed neutron precursors drift with the fuel salt. The steady-state consequences — a reduced effective delayed neutron fraction — are well captured by system codes, but the reactivity of the drift has been available only on a single exponential mode or, on-line, only at constant power, where it equals the inventory reading β 0 − β eff ( t ) . In power-varying transients that reading conflates the flow effect with ordinary precursor lag, and the built-in reactivity of the codes deliberately omits the drift channel. This paper derives a shadow-precursor observer that isolates the drift component as an on-line equivalent reactivity for arbitrary power histories — one differential equation per precursor group, non-intrusive — together with an exponential-mode closed form and the circulating-fuel inhour relation for the core–loop geometry. A three-tier, experiment-free benchmark set executed in Modelica/TRANSFORM verifies all three against closed-form references in the code’s own discrete equations: the observer recovers the constant-power reading exactly and matches the inhour and exponential-mode references in free-power flow transients. Under a ＋50 pcm step at constant flow, the observer exposes a drift modulation of + 67.1 pcm, and the common static- β eff substitution overestimates the period of that insertion by + 28 % .

title: Investigation on organic Rankine cycle technology for utilizing low-temperature waste heat sources from fusion reactors
abstract: Fusion energy is recognized as one of the cleanest base-load power sources with abundant fuel reserves, inherent safety and near-zero carbon emissions, which is expected to fundamentally address global fossil energy depletion and climate change. Fusion reactors generate multi-grade waste heat covering wide temperature intervals: high-temperature heat from blanket modules can be matched with steam Rankine or supercritical CO 2 Brayton cycles, while massive low-temperature cooling waste heat below 200 °C is produced from divertor cooling loops and vacuum vessel heat dissipation. Such low-grade heat cannot be efficiently recovered by conventional high-temperature power cycles, resulting in substantial energy loss and constraining the overall energy utilization efficiency of fusion facilities. To address this bottleneck, this paper establishes an Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) thermodynamic model coupled with the REFPROP fluid property database for recovering fusion low-temperature waste heat, and systematically performs thermal performance evaluation and component-level exergy analysis on ten typical organic working fluids including alkanes, dimethyl ether and fluorinated refrigerants within the heat source range of 80-180 °C. The simulation results indicate that evaporating temperature serves as the dominant parameter governing cycle thermal efficiency, exergy efficiency and circulating mass flow rate. With the rise of evaporator outlet temperature, thermal efficiency and exergy efficiency increase rapidly, whereas the required working fluid mass flow rate decreases monotonically. Under identical operating conditions, R1234ze(E) requires the maximum circulation flow rate of 10.349 kg/s, while pentane and isopentane exhibit the lowest flow rates of 3.359 kg/s and 3.505 kg/s repectively. For full-range heat sources (80-180 °C), pentane, isopentane and R123 deliver balanced superior thermodynamic performance; R123 exhibits the maximum thermal efficiency of 16.86 % at at an evaporation temperature of 170 °C.R1234ze(E), R134a, R152a and dimethyl ether are alternative candidates exclusive to heat sources below 100 °C. R245fa owns mature industrial supporting technology but is limited by its high Global Warming Potential (GWP) and narrow applicable temperature range. Sensitivity analysis reveals that the variation of expander isentropic efficiency imposes far more significant impacts on system performance than pump efficiency. Second-law exergy decomposition indicates that evaporator and condenser are the two dominant exergy destruction sources of the whole system, while pump exergy loss remains negligible. Comprehensive comparison covering thermodynamic characteristics, environmental friendliness and operation adaptability suggests pentane and isopentane are the optimal matching working fluids for the proposed fusion waste heat ORC system, featuring low total exergy dissipation, minimal circulation flow and mild environmental hazards. This work provides quantitative reference for working fluid screening and heat exchanger structural optimization of fusion low-grade heat recovery ORC systems, and offers clear optimization priorities targeted at core irreversible loss components.

title: Development of an improved solidification model for molten salt reactor applications
abstract: The freezing of molten salt in flow systems is one of the major safety concerns for molten salt reactors (MSRs), since solidification in drain lines or passive heat removal systems can obstruct emergency cooling lines and trigger uncontrolled temperature excursions in the reactor core. To predict this behavior, an improved solidification model is developed, which can be adopted in thermal-hydraulic system codes. Building on an existing fuel salt freezing formulation, the present model adds an energy equation for the pipe wall to restore the wall thermal inertia that the earlier model neglects. The governing equations are cast in control-volume form with semi-implicit numerical solution and solved in a MATLAB program for assessment. The model is first applied to the conceptual FLiBe and water cases, where it reproduces the existing model without the wall and predicts slower freezing once the wall thermal inertia is included. The model is then validated against dynamic and static water-freezing experiments and showing better agreement with measured data than the reference models. The results indicate that the proposed model captures the physics of molten salt freezing and provides a useful basis for MSR safety analysis within the MARS code.

title: Partially closed nuclear fuel cycle strategy integrating a NuScale-like reactor and an Accelerator Driven System (ADS)
abstract: This study proposes a partially closed nuclear fuel cycle that integrates a NuScale-like reactor with an adapted Accelerator-Driven System (ADS) through a three-stage approach. NuScale first produces spent fuel, which is reprocessed using the GANEX technique and loaded into the ADS-SMR, a smaller version of the ADS reactor geometrically adapted to match the NuScale dimensions and to incorporate the seed-blanket-unit (SBU) concept. Initially, the ADS-SMR arrangement contains reprocessed fuel in the seed region and thorium dioxide in the blanket region, aiming at fuel regeneration. This thorium-after-breeding fuel is then progressively loaded back into the three batch positions of the NuScale core designed for fresh fuel insertion during reshuffling, thereby resulting in three models with distinct fuel loading patterns. Results showed that the effective multiplication factor from the ADS-SMR dropped slightly over ten years, even without additional fissile input during the operation time. It also generated significant 233 U, reaching about 5.82 wt% fissile content. Back to the NuScale reactor, the three models exhibited early criticality increases due to in-situ fissile breeding, with one of the models nearly doubling energy output per kgHM compared to the reference case. Overall, the study highlights a feasible path for a partially closed nuclear fuel cycle strategy integrating ADS and SMR technologies. The Serpent code version 2.1.32, developed by VTT, and the ENDF/B-VII.0 nuclear data library have been used to perform the simulations.

title: Impact of neutron spectrum and burnability on the selection of spectral shift absorbers for space nuclear reactors
abstract: To ensure subcriticality during launch abort accidents while minimizing operational reactivity penalties, Spectral Shift Absorbers (SSAs) are essential for space nuclear reactors. However, existing SSA selection studies are often limited to specific reactor designs and neglect the effects of lifetime burnability, thereby limiting the general applicability and reliability of their conclusions. In this work, the comparative analysis of SSA effectiveness is conducted for three representative reactors with different neutron energy spectra. Five candidate SSAs, including 151 Eu 2 O 3 , 155 Gd 2 O 3 , 157 Gd 2 O 3 , 10 B 4 C, and 151 Eu 10 B 6 , are evaluated. Two mission profiles, 1 MWth and 5 MWth for 10 years, are considered to analyze burnability effects. The results indicate that SSA effectiveness is strongly dependent on the reactor neutron spectrum. The effectiveness ranking can be explained by a proposed spectral crossover mechanism, which governs the balance between accident flux suppression and operational flux penalty. Furthermore, SSA burnability influences end-of-life performance, thereby changing the SSA effectiveness rankings. As a result, 10 B 4 C surpasses 151 Eu 2 O 3 as the superior SSA in the Reactor C with high burnup profiles. Besides, although 157 Gd 2 O 3 exhibits poor burnability in the fast spectra, it offers superior performance in the Reactor B where the crossover energy aligns with the resonance region. These findings demonstrate that both spectrum characteristics and burnability behavior have important influences in SSA selection, providing generalized guidance for future space reactor designs.
title_ko: 중성자 스펙트럼과 연소성이 우주 핵 원자로의 스펙트럼 이동 흡수체 선택에 미치는 영향

title: Experimental study on thermal cycling phenomena and load response in downward-horizontal (DH) stagnant branch pipes of nuclear power plants
abstract: Thermal cycling phenomena refer to periodic fluctuations of the cold-hot interface in pipes of nuclear power plants, which induce temperature fluctuations and cause fatigue damage, threatening long-term operational safety. The downward-horizontal (DH) stagnant branch pipe is commonly found in nuclear power plants and is particularly susceptible to this phenomenon. Several related incidents have been reported internationally, making it necessary to study its characteristics for developing engineering protection strategies. This study investigated thermal cycling phenomena in a DH stagnant branch pipe using a high-temperature, high-pressure thermal-hydraulic test facility. The geometry of the test section was designed through numerical simulation and iterative debugging to capture thermal cycling in a large stagnant branch pipe, and pipe wall temperatures and strains at key locations were measured synchronously. The synchronous measurement provides direct experimental evidence of the cyclic loading induced by thermal cycling, which in previous studies was mainly inferred from numerical simulations. Experiments covered steady and pulsating flow conditions, with temperatures ranging from 60 to 260 °C and main pipe flow velocities from 3.1 to 10 m/s. analysis of data from 14 test cases shows that, under typical conditions, thermal cycling exhibits a sawtooth-shaped fluctuation characterized by rapid rise, temporary stabilization, and slow decline, with superimposed multi-time-scale variations. Under thermal cycling, pipe wall stresses at the elbow and horizontal sections show highly synchronized periodic fluctuations with temperature, confirming that the phenomenon generates significant fatigue loading on the structure. The cold-hot mixing region can be divided into three distinct zones along the pipe, whose extents are influenced by the temperature and flow velocity of the main pipe. Excessively low or high temperature differences between the main and branch pipes both dampen the fluctuations, the former for insufficient mixing drive and the latter for buoyancy-dominated suppression. Within a sensitive intermediate temperature-difference range, however, the cold-hot interface becomes unstable due to turbulent penetration and heat dissipation, leading to complex flows and intensified fluctuations. A higher steady main pipe velocity enhances turbulent penetration, while a pulsating main flow causes the cold-hot interface to undergo repeated reconstruction-breakdown-reconstruction cycles, amplifying flow instability and significantly increasing temperature and load fluctuations. Dynamic flow variations should therefore be avoided during plant operation. The results provide experimental data and a mechanistic basis for the numerical validation, fatigue assessment, and engineering protection of DH stagnant branch pipes against thermal cycling

title: A comparative study on MELCOR and MAAP simulations of a severe accident scenario in a Nordic boiling water reactor
abstract: This study juxtaposes the results from two independent simulations of a station blackout scenario in a Nordic boiling water reactor (BWR) using the MAAP and MELCOR codes. The purpose is to better understand and analyse code differences in general and the existing MELCOR and MAAP models of a Nordic boiling water reactor (BWR) in particular. The figures of merit in the comparative study are chronology of events till the actuation of filtered containment venting (FCV), corium temperature and relocation, reactor pressure vessel (RPV) pressure, containment pressure and hydrogen generation. Observed from the limited scope of comparisons, the overall accident progression and the failures of fuels and RPV lower head are consistent with the findings of the MAAP-MELCOR crosswalk study previously performed by EPRI and Sandia National Laboratories ( Luxat et al., 2016 ; Andrews et al., 2017 ). The MELCOR model predicted a later vessel breach and melt ejection into the containment than the MAAP model did, while the MAAP model predicted earlier actuation of the FCV system even though the MELCOR model showed a faster containment pressure increase after RPV failure due to greater hydrogen accumulation. The two codes also differed in their predictions of post-venting containment response, with the MELCOR simulation featuring a significant containment pressure oscillation with a cyclic period of 3–4 h, caused by difference in modelling of pool hydrodynamics in the lower drywell and the wetwell. Since containment pressure evolution is important to safety, this phenomenon merits further investigation.

title: Simulation and exergy analysis of the EPR nuclear power plant
abstract: A detailed energy and exergy assessment of the European Pressurized Reactor (EPR) plant is conducted to evaluate its thermodynamic performance and identify opportunities for efficiency improvement. Simulations of both the primary and secondary circuits were performed using the DWSIM process simulation software with the CoolProp property package. The predicted overall energy efficiency of the plant reaches 39% at a condenser temperature of 30°C, while the exergy efficiency of the secondary circuit is estimated at 77%. When the reactor core is included in the analysis, the overall exergy efficiency declines to 39%, close to the energy efficiency, revealing that most of the exergy destruction arises from irreversible nuclear-to-thermal energy conversion. The study highlights the contrast between energy and exergy perspectives: most energy losses occur at the condenser, while the secondary circuit is highly optimized in terms of exergy, and the nuclear reactor is the site of the largest exergy destruction. Coupling the EPR with a Rankine bottoming cycle using appropriate working fluids allows significant recovery of condenser waste heat, yielding a substantial increase of the electrical power output.

title: Mass analysis of supercritical nitrous oxide and helium in a recompression Brayton cycle utilizing in-situ resources for lunar base energy system
abstract: The Moon is the only natural satellite of the Earth and also the closest celestial body to the Earth. The Moon is regarded as an outpost of deep space exploration. The construction of lunar base infrastructure, polar exploration, and rovers constitutes the first step for humans to venture into the Moon. In the process of constructing a lunar base, it is essential to establish an energy system that can fully utilize local resources. This system will reduce the weight of materials transported from Earth and ultimately solve the energy shortage problem on the Moon. A recompression Brayton cycle that utilizes in-situ resources, with supercritical nitrous oxide and helium as the working media, and evaluates the mass of the energy system. A small modular reactor is applied to predict the minimum-mass reactor suitable for the given cycle conditions. The system mass and specific mass optimization explored the trade-offs among the reactor, radiation shield, Brayton cycle unit, recuperator, and radiator to obtain the minimum mass of the lunar base energy system. The results indicate that the specific mass of the energy system is 17.37 kg∙kWe −1 . In addition, it is found that, by utilizing in-situ lunar base resources, the mass and volume of the radiation shield for the reactor can be reduced by 3.55% and 14.20%, respectively. In conclusion, the proposed energy system scheme offers several advantages, including light weight, high efficiency, and continuous electricity supply, for application in lunar bases.

title: Interpretability study on generalization ability of data-driven fault diagnosis methods under domain shifts for nuclear power plants: From the perspective of data representations
abstract: The generalization ability of data–driven fault diagnosis models is critically challenged in Nuclear Power Plants (NPPs) due to domain shifts arising from varying operating conditions. In existing studies, model generalization ability is primarily enhanced through modifications to model architectures or learning algorithms, whereas the impact of data representations on generalization ability is rarely investigated. To address the above limitations, an integrated framework is proposed to analyze the impact of data representations on generalization ability and the potential mechanisms. By constructing different representations of the raw data through various feature scaling methods, the impact of data representations on model generalization ability is assessed via systematic training and evaluation. Furthermore, the mechanisms by which data representations influence model generalization ability are elucidated by SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)-based interpretability analysis from both global and local perspectives. Distinct feature–dependence patterns across trained models are induced by disparities in the relative distributions of Domain–Invariant Features (DIFs) and Domain–Sensitive Features (DSFs), thereby resulting in variations in generalization ability. By systematically characterizing the influence of data representations on model generalization ability and elucidating the potential mechanisms that lead to performance variations, novel insights and practical guidance are provided for enhancing the generalization ability of fault diagnosis models in NPPs, which can be achieved by obtaining more generalizable data representations through optimized feature scaling methods.
title_ko: 원자력 발전소에 대한 영역 이동 하에서의 데이터 기반 고장 진단 방법의 일반화 능력에 대한 해석성 연구: 데이터 표현의 관점에서

title: Adaptive spatial convolution weight window smoothing for global variance reduction in deep-penetration Monte Carlo simulations
abstract: In deep-penetration Monte Carlo simulations, the efficiency of the weight window global variance reduction (WWGVR) method critically depends on the accuracy of the lower weight window bounds. Statistical fluctuations during the initial iterations of self-coupled Monte Carlo method often lead to biased weight window estimates, triggering long-history problems. Conventional practice relies on empirical parameters as mandatory constraints. However, these parameters exert limited influence on Figure-of-Merit (FOM) within reasonable ranges, indicating that the efficiency bottleneck lies not in parameter fine-tuning but in the rationality of the weight window distribution. To address this, an Adaptive Spatial Convolution Weight Window Smoothing (ASCWWS) method is proposed, which employs an error-adaptive neighbourhood convolution kernel to achieve low-pass filtering and regularization of the weight window field, transforming point estimation into field estimation to suppress high-frequency noise and restore physically consistent importance gradients. Validation on the HBR-2 and EURACOS benchmarks shows that ASCWWS improves the FOM by factors of 1.86 and 4.06 compared to the conventional MAGIC method, respectively, with the incidence of importance inversion reduced by over 31%. By enhancing weight window distribution quality, ASCWWS reduces reliance on empirical parameters and can be directly integrated into existing self-coupled Monte Carlo method frameworks as a post-processing tool, offering a new pathway for efficient WWGVR simulation of deep-penetration problems.
title_ko: 심층 침투 몬테카를로 시뮬레이션에서 전체 분산 감소를 위한 적응형 공간 컨볼루션 가중치 윈도우 스무딩

title: Thermal-hydraulic analysis of rotated wire wrap in LFR assembly under normal operation and flow blockage conditions
abstract: This study presents a CFD investigation of thermal-hydraulic behavior in a 19-pin wire-wrapped lead-based fast reactor (LFR) fuel assembly under normal operation and flow blockage conditions. The numerical model is validated against the NACIE-UP ADP10 experiment using the SST k-ω turbulence model, with temperature and pressure drop comparisons confirming grid independence. Two heating modes (uniform and central) and four rotation angles of the central wire wrap (60° and 120° clockwise and counterclockwise) are considered. Results show that wire rotation modifies radial coolant paths and degrades near-wall heat transfer, causing localized temperature rises that are more pronounced under central heating. Subsequently, two blockage cases are simulated under central heating at different axial positions. Although blockage effects on temperature distribution become negligible after flow recovery, at the blockage end, peak temperatures can increase by up to 51 K depending on rotation angle and axial location, and the extent of the disturbed flow region also varies. These findings underscore the need for enhanced attention to local thermal-hydraulic safety when rotated wire wraps and blockage accidents coexist.
title_ko: 정상 작동 및 유동 차단 조건에서 LFR 어셈블리에서 회전 와이어 랩의 열수력 분석

title: Operational characteristics of the experimental test facility for the passive cooling system of spent fuel pools
abstract: Ensuring reliable removal of residual heat from spent fuel pools is a key safety requirement for nuclear facilities, particularly for research reactors where the safe storage of spent fuel assemblies must be maintained under both normal and accident conditions. This paper presents the results of experimental studies of a test facility for a passive residual heat removal system designed for spent fuel assemblies in the spent fuel pool of a research nuclear reactor. The study employed both theoretical and empirical methods. The article describes the main thermal-hydraulic parameters and design features of the test facility and provides a description of the experimental methodology. The results of tests carried out under various operating modes of the facility are presented, including operation with full and partial filling of the circuit with the working fluid and operation in an annular thermosyphon mode. The experimental results confirm the operability of the proposed design and demonstrate the capability of the system to provide effective heat removal under different thermal conditions. In addition, three-dimensional modeling of the test facility was performed, which made it possible to identify design characteristics of components not accessible to visual inspection and to optimize the configuration of the evaporator module to ensure a more uniform distribution of the working fluid flow. A theoretical assessment of the impact of using this facility as part of a passive heat removal system on nuclear safety when installed in a spent fuel pool is also provided. The obtained results indicate that the installation of the proposed system does not lead to a violation of nuclear safety requirements and can serve as a basis for the development of a full-scale passive cooling system for spent fuel pools of research reactors.
title_ko: 소비 연료 풀의 수동 냉각 시스템을 위한 실험 테스트 시설의 작동 특성

title: Impact of possible nuclear phase-out strategies in Spain for a sustainable energy transition
abstract: Spain's long-term energy strategy combines rapid renewable expansion with the progressive phase-out of nuclear power by 2035. Since the timing of reactor retirements can significantly affect the long-term electricity balance, this study compares four nuclear phase-out scenarios: the current official retirement schedule (SCN_40) and three lifetime-extension pathways allowing reactor operation up to 50, 55, and 60 years (SCN_50, SCN_55, and SCN_60, respectively). All scenarios use the same demand and renewable deployment trajectories. A target-driven daily simulation developed with LEAF-EB combines historical generation and demand patterns with projections derived from the PNIEC and Spain's long-term decarbonization strategy. For each scenario, 1000 Monte Carlo simulations estimate clean electricity surpluses and the raw clean generation gap. Surpluses are allocated to BESS charging, exports, and synthetic methane production, while the gap is covered by BESS discharge, cross-border imports, methane reconversion, and residual backup. Over 2028–2050, extending reactor operation from the official schedule to 60 years reduces the modeled cumulative clean generation gap by 39.1% and electricity imports by 38.5%, while exports increase by 72.4%. BESS discharge covers 7.2–11.4% of the gap, while imports account for approximately 21% across all scenarios. Electricity recovered from stored synthetic methane increases from 77.2 to 153.2 TWh, raising its contribution from 8.1% in SCN_40 to 26.5% in SCN_60. The residual backup requirement decreases by 61.0%, from 599.3 to 233.5 TWh, but still covers 40.4% of the gap in SCN_60 and is required on 14.0% of simulated days. Extending nuclear operation therefore reduces the magnitude and frequency of balancing requirements but does not eliminate the need for firm backup generation under the modeled assumptions.
title_ko: 지속 가능한 에너지 전환을 위한 스페인의 가능한 핵 단계적 폐기 전략의 영향

title: Design of liquid lead-bismuth eutectic flow velocity measurement based on contactless inductive flow tomography
abstract: liquid lead-bismuth eutectic (LBE) serves as the coolant for lead-cooled fast reactors (LFR), its velocity distribution is a critical parameter in thermal-hydraulic research. However, the high-temperature corrosivity and opacity of LBE pose significant challenges to the application of traditional flow velocity measurement methods. To address this issue, this study applies Contactless Inductive Flow Tomography (CIFT) and designs a measurement system applicable for LBE flow velocity measurement. The validity of the proposed measurement scheme is verified by comparing the reference velocity field with the velocity field reconstructed via the reconstruction algorithm. Maintaining a comparable total number of sensors, we compare three spatial arrangements: 12×4, 10×5, and 8×6. The results indicate that the 8×6 arrangement achieves the highest degree of agreement between the reconstructed and reference velocity field. Furthermore, the applicability of this measurement system is verified under noisy condition and within complex flow field. The proposed design scheme and sensor configuration analysis provide a valuable reference for the future application of CIFT in LBE flow measurement.

title: Conceptual study of a supercritical CO2-cooled, triply periodic minimal surface lattice-based microreactor
abstract: Advancements in additive manufacturing (AM) processes have made it increasingly feasible to consider optimized shapes such as triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattices for heat transfer applications, ranging from heat exchanger designs to nuclear fuel elements. This study introduces a TPMS-lattice-shaped nuclear core and compares its performance against that of a traditional pin-based design. A publicly available design that relies on typical fuel pin elements for a fast spectrum, supercritical CO 2 (sCO 2 )-cooled reactor with a direct Brayton cycle was selected as the reference design. The same core materials were used in the TPMS core to ensure a fair comparison between both geometries. Due to the complexity of this type of geometry, innovative modeling strategies were introduced. The thermal performance of the TPMS fuel element was analyzed using a computational scheme that combined high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with Multiphysics Object-Oriented Simulation Environment (MOOSE)-based 1D thermal hydraulics, coupled with 3D heat transfer. Monte Carlo reactor physics analyses using unstructured meshes in Serpent were employed to characterize the core performance and verified against a native constructive solid geometry TPMS lattice implementation in OpenMC. When it comes to fast spectrum reactors, TPMS geometries are neutronically equivalent to pin geometries. However, TPMS-based fuel elements offer improved heat transfer performance, enabling the power density to be increased up to 59% while still meeting the peak material temperature requirements. A downside of TPMS lattices is the additional pressure drop per unit length, which may be manageable when factoring the pumping power costs into the total energy generated by the proposed microreactor concept.

title: Network Algorithm-Based Implications of Nuclear Energy Capacity Expansion for Climate Mitigation
abstract: This study aims to develop an advanced, AI-driven System Dynamics model utilizing the Internet of Everything (IoE) to evaluate the impact of tripling nuclear energy capacity on climate change mitigation in alignment with the 28th Conference of the Parties (COP28) objectives. The Internet of Things (IoT), a network of interconnected devices, has been employed for computer system communication. The IoE extends this concept to encompass a more interconnected world, integrating processes, data, objects, and individuals. A dynamic simulation of 100 months was conducted, examining the interactions of Things, People, Data, and Processes. While the classification of Things increased steadily, the People category exhibited two distinct peaks at the 30th and 55th months, with false positives (FP) outnumbering Ttue positives (TP), false negatives (FN), and true negatives (TN). FN and TN demonstrated comparable trends. The Data category increased gradually across all classifications, while Processes declined with sporadic drops. A comparison of Recall (RC) and Precision (PC) shows consistently higher RC values, with People achieving the highest overall. These findings offer actionable insights for large-scale IoT and IoE systems in energy, manufacturing, transportation, and smart cities. Trends like steady growth in Things and Data, human-system volatility, and the importance of recalibration help organizations optimize system design, reduce errors, and improve smart infrastructure adaptability.

title: Comprehensive Atomistic Investigation of the Structural and Thermodynamic Properties of CrUO4 and Cr2UO6
abstract: ABSTRACT In this study, spin-polarized DFT+U calculations were performed to investigate thermo-mechanical properties and irradiation-induced defect evolution of CrUO 4 and Cr 2 UO 6 compounds within the Cr-U-O system. It should be noted that these two phases are treated as independent, hypothetical chemical entities in the present work. The calculated lattice parameters deviate from experimental and theoretical data by 1-2%, an acceptable range for actinide oxide simulations. Both compounds exhibit distinct mechanical anisotropy: orthorhombic Cr 2 UO 6 strongly resist uniaxial compression, while hexagonal CrUO 4 has orientation-dependent elastic stiffness. Plasticity indices ( δ = B / C 44 ) confirm their good ductility, and 3D analyses further verify anisotropy in elastic moduli, Poisson’s ratio and hardness. Total and partial density of states reveal the bonding contributions of Cr 3 d , U 5 f and O 2 p orbitals. We also calculated thermodynamic parameters and point defect energies. Chromium interstitials are energetically favorable in both phases, unlike oxygen interstitials dominant in pure UO 2 . Interstitial defects show negative trap energies, where uranium vacancies possess the highest values. This work offers fundamental theoretical data for understanding the intrinsic behaviors of CrUO 4 and Cr 2 UO 6 themselves, which may provide indirect reference for broader studies on advanced Cr-doped UO 2 nuclear fuel systems.

title: Research on irradiation-Thermo-mechanical coupled analysis for HTGR fuels
abstract: Predicting the thermo-mechanical response of TRISO particle fuel is important for fuel performance assessment in high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. This study developed CoaPAC (COated fuel Performance Analysis Code), a spherical TRISO fuel performance code that couples implicit heat transfer, fission gas and CO release, viscoelastic coating mechanics, gap evolution, and pressure-vessel (PV)-type failure models. First, CoaPAC was benchmarked against the IAEA CRP-6 mechanical test case, and its results were compared with published results from other fuel performance codes for the HFR P4, HFR-EU1, and NPR-1 irradiation conditions. The results show that CoaPAC reproduces the principal evolution trends of key thermo-mechanical variables, and the comparisons support the consistency of the basic physical modules and their coupled implementation. CoaPAC was then applied to a complex full-life-cycle scenario involving irradiation, storage, and accident heating. The results demonstrate that, under a continuous and complex operating history, CoaPAC can reasonably describe the coupled responses of TRISO particles, including heat transfer, gas composition, coating stress, and failure behavior at different stages. Therefore, the verification and comparison analyses conducted in this study support the accuracy and reliability of the code, demonstrate the reasonableness of its thermo-mechanical model implementation and its capability to handle complex conditions, and further clarify priorities for future code development.

title: Numerical study on direct contact condensation of countercurrent subcooled water-steam flow in a steam-filled vertical rectangular narrow channel
abstract: A two-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model was developed to investigate direct contact condensation (DCC) during counter-current flow of subcooled water and steam in a steam-filled vertical rectangular narrow channel. The model incorporates the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method, Lee phase-change model, Continuum Surface Force (CSF) model, and RNG k–ε turbulence model. The effects of subcooled-water and steam inlet velocities on flow evolution, pressure response, and counter-current flow limitation (CCFL) were systematically analyzed. The results show that the channel pressure exhibits pronounced periodic pulsations. Increasing the inlet velocities of both phases strengthens interfacial shear and flow disturbances, thereby intensifying interfacial instability, promoting condensation-induced water hammer (CIWH), and increasing the pressure oscillation intensity. The maximum pressure is mainly controlled by the subcooled-water inlet velocity and increases monotonically with it, while steam injection markedly amplifies the pressure peak compared with single-phase liquid injection. The average pressure increases with either inlet velocity, with the liquid velocity exerting a stronger effect. Flooding and liquid-bridge formation are observed during counter-current flow, triggering CCFL. As the subcooled-water-to-steam velocity ratio increases, CCFL weakens, whereas higher steam velocities lead to earlier liquid-bridge formation.

title: Numerical study on debris bed formation characteristics following the FCI of a nuclear reactor severe accident with the EMPS method
abstract: Debris bed formation during fuel-coolant interaction (FCI) is a key process in the analysis of severe nuclear reactor accidents. Existing numerical studies typically decouple melt jet breakup and debris bed formation, relying on idealized fragment shape assumptions. The present study conducts a continuous numerical simulation of the FCI process by coupling the Explicit Moving Particle Semi-implicit (EMPS) method with a Contoured Continuum Surface Force (CCSF) model, a fragment identification model, and a Passively Moving Solid (PMS) model. The integrated approach tracks the dynamic evolution from initial melt injection and solidification to final bed accumulation. The established numerical model is validated against experimental data, with macroscopic predictions showing consistency with physical measurements. Parametric analyses reveal the mechanisms governing debris bed morphology. Increasing the LBE temperature, jet velocity, and water temperature increases the spreading area. High LBE and water temperatures induce edge crust remelting and secondary expansion. Furthermore, the debris bed accumulation height decreases as these three parameters increase. The total porosity increases with elevated LBE temperatures and jet velocities, and decreases under higher cooling water temperatures. The proposed modeling approach provides quantitative insight into debris bed formation and may support the development of severe accident management strategies.

title: Evaluation of time-dependent background in neutron time-of-flight transmission measurements using a 6Li-glass scintillation detector
abstract: Accurate evaluation of time-dependent background is essential for reliable neutron time-of-flight (TOF) transmission measurements in neutron resonance analysis (NRA). In this study, we experimentally investigated the time-dependent background in neutron transmission measurements utilizing a 6 Li-glass scintillation detector at the Kyoto University, Institute for Integrated Radiation and Nuclear Science - Linear Accelerator (KURNS-LINAC). A comparative analysis was conducted on three background evaluation techniques, namely the black resonance, neutron absorber, and pulse-height (PH) gate techniques under identical measurement conditions. The results demonstrated that background levels obtained with resonance filters or neutron absorbers can be underestimated due to gamma-ray attenuation by the inserted materials. Conversely, the PH gate technique can overestimate the background in the thermal energy range due to gamma-rays produced by the capture of scattered thermal neutrons. Herein, the characteristics, advantages, and limitations of each technique are discussed, and practical guidance for selecting appropriate techniques and corrections to achieve accurate background evaluation in neutron transmission measurements using a 6 Li-glass scintillation detector is presented, supporting improved resonance analysis for future NRA applications.

title: Core characteristics of a modified pebble-bed high-temperature gas-cooled reactor design
abstract: As a promising candidate of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) proves its technical superiority and maturity with the successful commercial operation of Chinese High Temperature gas-cooled Reactor Pebble-bed Module (HTR-PM) in Shidao Bay, Shandong. HTR-PM employs an online-refueling pebble-bed reactor design. Spherical fuel elements enter the core through the top fueling tube, gradually move downward through the pebble bed, and are discharged via the bottom defueling tube. Simultaneously, the coolant enters the pressure vessel and flows around its periphery before reaching the cold helium plenum at the top of the core. It then cools the pebble core in a top-down flow, merges in the hot helium plenum at the bottom, and finally exits the pressure vessel. Based on the design of the HTR-PM, a modified core design (HTR-UD) is proposed, featuring a top-down movement of spherical fuel elements and a bottom-up flow of coolant. This design leverages the strong negative temperature feedback in HTGR to flatten the axial power distribution within the core. A comparative analysis of the core characteristics between the two designs is conducted, and two core upgrading schemes are investigated for the HTR-UD. The analysis results indicate that the HTR-UD can significantly reduce the maximum fuel temperature by approximately 175 °C under depressurized loss of forced cooling (DLOFC) accident. Furthermore, it demonstrates the potential to increase the thermal power by approximately 40% or increase the reactor outlet coolant temperature to 900 °C compared to the original HTR-PM design.

title: An evaluation of diffusivity and resolution models for fission gas release in UO2
abstract: Gas atom behavior is of particular interest to nuclear reactor designers as it plays a key role in determining fission gas release and fuel swelling. Various models have been developed for both the diffusivity and resolution of fission gas in UO 2 for use in fuel performance codes, including both empirical models fitted to experimental data and mechanistic models that represent physical behaviors. This work establishes a consistent methodology for comparing empirical and mechanistic diffusivity and resolution models by evaluating their impact on calculated fission gas release in BISON for several integral light water reactor irradiation experiments. Model accuracies are assessed by comparing the BISON-calculated release with the final fission gas release from the irradiation experiments. Bland–Altman analyses of each combination of models indicate that the mechanistic combination of Matthews diffusivity and Setyawan resolution, with other input parameters fixed, has a lower bias of -0.028% FGR than the historically used empirical pairing, the Turnbull-D1–D2–D3 diffusivity with White resolution, which produces a bias of -1.938% FGR. These results provide a comparative basis for selecting diffusivity and resolution models and suggest that mechanistic models can improve agreement with integral irradiation experiments while offering a more physically based framework for predicting fission gas release beyond the existing experimental database.

title: Numerical study of flow distribution and the effect of unsteady flow of liquid sodium coolant in annular rods scalloped-wall fuel assembly
abstract: The core of small sodium-cooled fast reactors is designed to be compact, meeting various regulatory and economic objectives. Heat removal in a compact core can be enhanced by using a tightly arranged annular rod fuel assembly within a scalloped-wall duct. This study investigates the steady and periodic flow of liquid sodium coolant through the triangular tight lattice ( P/D = 1.08) annular rod scalloped-wall fuel assembly. The scalloped wall reduced the temperature difference between the center subchannel and gaps by up to 30% compared to a flat-walled fuel assembly. The flow split between the inner and outer subchannels is 10% – 13% in the fuel assembly. The relationship between the Reynolds number and flow friction resistance aligns with previous results for a light water reactor fuel assembly. Periodic flow intensifies the turbulence distribution within the subchannels. A new correlation was proposed for the flow split between the inner and outer subchannels in the tight triangular-lattice scalloped-wall annular rod fuel assembly.
