title: Effects of corrosion-product particle deposition on flow-induced vibration of an LBE-cooled wire-wrapped fuel rod bundle
abstract: Corrosion-product particles generated in lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE) coolant may be retained on wire-wrapped fuel assemblies, and different particle-laden conditions associated with wall retention may modify local fluid excitation. A computational fluid dynamics–discrete phase model–flow-induced vibration (CFD-DPM-FIV) framework combining the shear stress transport (SST) k–ω model and one-way fluid–structure coupling is developed for a seven-pin LBE-cooled wire-wrapped fuel assembly to investigate the effects of particle mass flow rate, inlet velocity, and diameter. Under the reference particle condition, 73.87% of wall-trapped particles are located on the fuel-rod cladding surface, while 12.68% and 13.46% are located on the wire-wrap surface and hexagonal duct wall. Particle diameter and inlet velocity mainly alter the surface distribution of retained particles, whereas particle mass flow rate mainly changes the particle supply to the bundle. Although the global thermal–hydraulic parameters vary only slightly, the vibration response is sensitive to particle-retention conditions. Compared with the particle-free case, the high particle mass-flow-rate and large-particle cases increase the maximum total deformation from 85.208 μm to about 99.0 μm and the maximum von Mises stress from 0.2976 MPa to about 0.360 MPa. At the center-rod midspan, the fluctuating root-mean-square (RMS) displacement increases from 12.573 to about 22.96 μm in the X direction and from 33.774 to about 63.13 μm in the Z direction, while the dominant response frequency remains near 22 Hz. These results indicate that deposition-prone particle conditions can amplify the predicted FIV response before severe macroscopic blockage develops.

title: An enquiry into noise-induced reactivity shifts in the point-kinetics equations
abstract: Neutron noise analysis within the point-kinetics model is traditionally formulated using linear response theory under small-amplitude sinusoidal perturbations. Although this approach has proven successful in providing a conceptual foundation for neutron noise measurement and diagnostics, it neglects potential non-linear effects that may, for example, modify the stationary state of the reactor. In particular, effective reactivity shifts can be generated by non-linear interactions, which are not captured by the standard linearized treatment. These effects are nevertheless generally assumed to remain negligible under deterministic forcing. This assumption may break down in the presence of stochastic fluctuations. Multiplicative noise can indeed induce systematic drift terms in the effective dynamics, leading to noise-induced reactivity shifts that drive the mean neutron population away from stationarity. The present work investigates the impact of non-linear neutron noise within the point-kinetics model, considering both deterministic and stochastic excitations. The magnitude of the resulting reactivity shifts is quantified, and the respective roles of stochastic forcing and delayed neutron precursors are analysed, providing an assessment of their potential operational significance. • Sinusoidal perturbations induces a reactivity shift of the neutron population. • Another reactivity shift is observed in the case of multiplicative noise. • Delayed neutrons introduce correlation-dependent drift.

title: Theoretical design and parametric sensitivity analysis of a passive containment cooling system based on separated heat pipes
abstract: A design-oriented inverse methodology is developed for a separated heat pipe passive containment cooling system (SHP-PCS) to determine feasible system configurations from prescribed accident heat removal requirements. A steady thermal-hydraulic sizing model is established by coupling heat transfer characteristics, two-phase flow pressure losses, natural circulation constraints, and engineering design limitations. The resulting configuration is further evaluated using a one-dimensional steady-state analysis model to investigate the effects of working fluid inventory, heat exchanger geometry, and riser dimensions on system performance. Two system-level heat removal requirements are considered, including a 50 MW high-pressure and high-temperature accident condition and a 12 MW long-term cooling condition. The designed separated heat pipe module is analyzed as the basic heat removal unit, and multiple modules can be integrated to satisfy the overall system requirements. The results show that the optimized configuration demonstrates the capability of passive heat removal under a relatively small source-sink elevation difference. The working fluid inventory exhibits a significant influence on system performance, with an optimal range of approximately 30–40%. The heat exchanger diameter shows an optimum due to the competition between hydraulic resistance reduction and heat transfer degradation, while riser diameter mainly affects system performance by changing vapor-side flow resistance. The proposed inverse-design framework provides a systematic approach for determining SHP-PCS configurations from required heat removal duties and provides engineering guidance for the optimization and application of separated heat pipe passive containment cooling systems.

title: High-fidelity prediction of LBE mixed convection heat transfer via gradient-balanced physics-informed neural networks
abstract: Mixed convection in liquid metals, such as lead-bismuth eutectic (LBE), presents intricate flow and heat transfer characteristics due to the strong coupling of forced and natural convection in low Prandtl number fluids. Accurately predicting these phenomena is paramount for the thermal-hydraulic safety and design of advanced nuclear reactors. In this study, a novel Mixed Convection Heat Transfer Physics-Informed Neural Network (MCHT-PINN) is proposed to conduct progressive case studies across a two-dimensional backward-facing step, a two-dimensional circular pipe, and a three-dimensional 19-pin fuel assembly. To address the highly coupled multi-physics fields, the MCHT-PINN architecture integrates the GradNorm adaptive-weight algorithm, which dynamically balances the loss gradients associated with the Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) and boundary conditions. The results demonstrate that the MCHT-PINN model achieves accurate predictions of both velocity and temperature fields, demonstrating excellent agreement with OpenFOAM reference solutions. The average relative L 2 errors are consistently maintained below 3% across all cases. Furthermore, the model accurately resolves complex coupled thermo-fluid phenomena, capturing not only buoyancy-driven velocity profile distortions but also the localized lifting of the thermal boundary layer and subsequent flow field evolution. Ultimately, these findings not only verify the robustness of the MCHT-PINN across varying geometries but also provide a reliable computational tool for evaluating complex thermal-hydraulics in liquid metal reactor components.

title: High-Fidelity Multiphysics Modeling of the Molten Salt Fast Reactor with Applications for Reduced-Order Models
abstract: The molten salt fast reactor (MSFR) is one of the six Generation-IV reactor designs. In the MSFR, the liquid fuel is also the coolant, which moves throughout the primary circuit. This complex phenomenology requires multiphysics modeling. In this paper, a high-fidelity model of the MSFR is developed in the multiphysics code Cardinal, accounting for neutronics–thermal-hydraulic feedback and the transport of delayed neutron precursors (DNPs) and decay heat precursors (DHPs).NekRS solves the mass, momentum, energy, and DNP and DHP transport equations. NekRS uses a Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes k−τ turbulence model. DNPs and DHPs are modeled using a convective diffusion equation with modified source terms that account for radioactive decay. OpenMC is used to solve the neutronics equation. Current limitations in OpenMC do not allow for the modification of delayed neutron source locations. Ongoing efforts look to include this feature in future work to introduce DNP feedback in OpenMC.The Cardinal results showed reasonable behavior for temperature, heat source, velocity, DNPs, and DHPs. In addition, the fission matrix (FM) method is used as a reduced-order neutronics model. The NekRS-FM model is analyzed and compared with the NekRS-OpenMC model. The results showed good agreement between the codes.

title: Topology optimization of the NaK78 inlet distributor for a liquid-cooled space nuclear reactor heat exchanger
abstract: Liquid-metal-cooled space nuclear reactors coupled with closed Brayton cycles are promising candidates for high-power deep-space missions. In these systems, the NaK78-to-He dual-fluid heat exchanger is critical. Yet, the concentrated liquid-metal inlet causes severe flow maldistribution, which can consume the limited pressure head (only 10–20% of that available from mechanical pumps) from electromagnetic pumps driving the NaK78 loop. Existing remedial measures rely on trial-and-error modifications to predefined geometric forms, offering no guarantee of optimality. In this work, we apply density-based topology optimization to autonomously determine the optimal solid baffle distribution within the NaK78 inlet plenum of a prototype space nuclear heat exchanger. The optimization is implemented in COMSOL Multiphysics 6.3 using Brinkman penalization and adjoint-based sensitivity analysis to minimize the integral of squared outlet velocity deviation. The inlet slot width is fixed at 8 mm ( Re ≈ 1980), ensuring the laminar flow assumption is strictly valid for this proof-of-concept study. Parametric investigations over solid volume fraction (φₛ = 0.3–0.7) and a uniformity-pressure-drop trade-off coefficient (C1 = 0–0.1 m −1 ) are conducted using β-continuation. The base-case optimized distributor achieves a coefficient of variation CV = 5.08% (uniformity index η = 0.949) and a pressure drop ΔP = 7.68 Pa, with φₛ = 0.5 identified as optimal. Notably, the uniformity-only objective (C1 = 0) is Pareto-dominant; increasing the pressure-drop penalty degrades both metrics simultaneously, a finding explained by the dual flow-organizing function of the curved baffles in the thin rectangular plenum. The optimizer autonomously discovers a curved bifurcating baffle topology physically analogous to wedge-shaped designs previously derived by empirical enumeration, yet obtained here rigorously and without geometric preconditioning. While the present 2D laminar model serves as a proof-of-concept, the discovered topology provides a physically meaningful baseline for future 3D turbulent validation under rated operating conditions. The present operating point corresponds to a thermal duty of approximately 6.8 kW; an order-of-magnitude assessment shows that remain laminar up to ∼500 kW(th) and only reaches transition at 1000 kW(th), while the inlet plenum becomes turbulent. This study establishes topology optimization as a systematic tool for inlet distributor design in liquid-metal nuclear heat exchangers, addressing the hydraulic root cause of maldistribution-induced thermal degradation.

title: Adaptive TD3-PID control for once-through steam generator using hardware-in-the-loop simulation
abstract: This paper presents a adaptive hybrid control framework that integrates Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) reinforcement learning with PID. This approach addresses the critical challenges of pronounced non-linearity, significant time delays, and wide-ranging operating conditions in the pressure control of Once-Through Steam Generators (OTSGs). By employing a TD3 agent to dynamically optimize PID within predefined safety bounds, the proposed strategy substantially improves system adaptability without compromising the inherent stability of the baseline PID structure. Extensive hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments on an industrial distributed control system (DCS) demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. Quantitative results show that the TD3-PID control reduces settling times by more than 50% during setpoint tracking. Moreover, under large-scale load transients, the intelligent agent suppresses pressure overshoot by 73%-90% and effectively attenuates associated temperature fluctuations. These results validate the robustness and practical feasibility of the proposed TD3-PID architecture, offering a viable pathway for the deployment of intelligent control systems in advanced nuclear energy applications.
title_ko: 하드웨어-인-더-루프 (hardware-in-the-loop) 시뮬레이션을 사용하는 원스루 스팀 발생기를 위한 적응형 TD3-PID 제어
